claims.claim: The CI diff failures reported in T-26271 (server-side apply dry-run on ClusterRole/cert-manager-cainjector rejected for a narrower identity, in projects that had just enabled the sync impersonation flag) are the direct consequence of RFC-001's implementation scope: the RFC wires the Impersonate configuration from the AppProject only into the Application Controller's sync path (sync.go setting SyncContext rawConfig/restConfig, and GitOps Engine honoring Impersonate for kubectl commands executed during sync), and selects the destinationServiceAccounts defaultServiceAccount per destination. Nothing in the RFC applies that identity to the diff/comparison path, and nothing in it says the diff identity changes when application.sync.impersonation.enabled is set, so the reporter's belief that the broad cluster Secret credential governs the diff is exactly what the design implies. The RFC's Risks and Mitigations section names only privilege escalation and does not acknowledge this diff-side effect.

T-28695 is the same design decision as T-26271 surfacing in the other component: sync honors destinationServiceAccounts while Server-Side Diff runs as the cluster Secret credential, because RFC-001 defines destinationServiceAccounts purely as sync-time impersonation configuration ('used for the sync operation for a particular destination cluster and namespace') and lists no change to the diff path in any of its Component sections (GitOps Engine, ArgoCD API, Application Controller, UI, CLI). The unbounded patch RBAC the ticket describes is the mechanism that follows: Server-Side Diff's dry-run apply is authorized as patch, so the least-privilege standing cluster credential that RFC-001 was written to make possible must instead be granted write authority on every resource kind. RFC-001 declares 'Non-Goals: None' and so never records that the diff path is out of scope.

T-27833's request — that namespace bootstrapping use the Argo CD control-plane service account while the sync of other resources uses the impersonated service account — is a symptom filed directly against RFC-001's stated granularity decision: 'The service account to be used for impersonation is determined on a per Application level rather than on per resource level,' with Application.spec.destination.namespace determining the single account for all resources in the Application. Combined with RFC-001's goal that the feature 'can be enabled/disabled only at the system level,' there is no seam at which kind: Namespace could be handled by a different identity than the rest of the sync, which is why the reporter's clusterResourceWhitelist and AppProject RBAC attempts leave the escape open.

The infinite delete/re-create loop in T-28511 is explained by the PRD's Reverse deletion semantics rather than by the AllAtOnce value shown in the ticket's reproduction YAML: the reporter notes the affected ApplicationSet configures a rollingSync step order plus the reverse deletion strategy, and the PRD defines Reverse as deleting in the reverse of the rollingSync steps order while it 'waits for one application to be fully deleted before moving onto the next application.' A child stuck Progressing means that wait never completes, so the sequential barrier never releases and the wave restarts from the top. The PRD's Risks and Mitigations section records 'No immediate Risks to consider' and specifies no timeout, no bounded wait, and no handling for an Application that cannot finish deleting.

The source-change churn described in T-27949 — the reporter is piloting the source hydrator on the same repository, and 'every hydration cycle lands a fresh commit on the hydrated branch that the child Applications deploy from, and each of those commits is picked up as a source change' — is the designed behavior of RFC-002, not an anomaly: the hydrator commits and pushes one hydrated commit per dry commit per syncSource.targetBranch group, and the application controller syncs whenever it detects a new hydrated commit on syncSource.targetBranch. RFC-002 has no debounce or coalescing mechanism beyond grouping a single dry commit's changes into one hydrated commit, and its Risks and Mitigations section is empty, so it never acknowledges the interaction with a RollingSync wave that treats each of those pushes as a new source revision.

T-26443's stale-manifest sync is a symptom of RFC-002's push-to-stage mode as designed: the ticket reports the problem is observed only in push-to-stage, where 'the external promoter has not yet moved the fresh manifests to the deployment branch,' and RFC-002 defines exactly that split — hydrated manifests go to the hydrateTo.targetBranch while the controller syncs from syncSource.targetBranch, and 'Argo CD relies on some external system to move changes to the deployment branch.' Because the controller's sync trigger is a new commit on syncSource.targetBranch and hydration writes elsewhere, an auto-sync app pointed at a reused branch applies whatever that branch last held. RFC-002 names the promotion system a Non-Goal and never states what the sync branch contains before the external system acts.

The unsigned-push failure in T-27327 ('This push happens outside the commit server, so if the target branch's SourceIntegrity policy requires verified signatures, the commit lands unsigned and the git host rejects the push') follows from RFC-002's decision that 'the actual push operation should be delegated to the commit server,' with write credentials held in the repository-write Secret the commit server consumes. Rollback's proposed git checkout / commit / push directly against the sync branch is outside that single delegated push path, so any signing or credential configuration attached to the commit server — the opt-in commitserver.sign.hydrated.commits key and commitserver.signing.key.path of T-28239 — cannot apply to it by construction.

The fleet-wide blast radius in T-28239's ops caveat — a rotated or expired signing key crash-loops commit-server startup and 'every hydrator-enabled app stops getting new commits' — is a property of RFC-002's architecture rather than of the signing feature: RFC-002 routes every hydrated push, for every Application and every targetBranch group, through the one CommitManifests call to the commit server. Because that component is the sole writer of hydrated branches, its fail-fast startup refusal converts a single cluster-wide key problem into a hydration outage for all apps, and RFC-002 never discusses commit server availability (its Risks and Mitigations section is empty).

T-24417's gap — DrySource cannot point at a chart in a Helm repository, and the reporter would have to switch to Helm dependencies — is precisely what RFC-002 decided: 'The spec.sourceHydrator.drySource field contains only three fields: repoURL, targetRevision, and path,' and RFC-002 explicitly rejected preserving the multi-source style of external chart/values inclusion, stating 'we'll recommend that users use the umbrella chart approach' because it 'felt like we were re-implementing Helm's dependencies feature.' The ticket's second requirement, allowing SyncSource and HydrateTo to point at a different repository, collides with the same design: RFC-002 has Argo CD 'watch two revisions in the same git repository.'
